frame: "Cattle" + a prepositional phrase ending on a plural noun; tense from a provided-that clause whose subject is singular
decider_quote: provided that the herd's drinking water comes
deletion_test: Delete "provided that the herd's drinking water comes from piped springs": "Cattle on the upland farms were safe from infection" (the result of last spring's screening) and "are safe" (a general finding) are both acceptable; "let" in the last clause is the same form in present and past, so nothing else fixes the tense.

distractor_pulls.is safe: The first sentence uses "livestock was": the student has just seen the farm-animal noun take a singular verb, and "Cattle" (no -s) looks like the same kind of mass noun; "the herd's" later is singular too.
distractor_pulls.were safe: The passage opens with a past screening ("was screened last spring"), so reporting what it found in the past reads naturally, and the number is right.
distractor_pulls.was safe: It repeats the first sentence's verb word for word ("livestock was"), which looks like careful parallelism with the same subject matter.

distractor_kills.is safe: Agreement: "cattle" is a plural noun ("these cattle are"); correct only with a mass or singular subject: "Livestock on the upland farms is safe."
distractor_kills.were safe: Tense consistency: a main clause governed by the present-tense condition "provided that ... water comes" must be present; correct only with "provided that ... water came."
distractor_kills.was safe: Fails both number and tense; correct only in "Livestock was safe provided that its water came from springs."

hostile_reader.options_only_pick: none: a 2x2 with one shared word
hostile_reader.changed: revision: removed "the animals drink" (a plural restatement that handed over both number and tense); the condition's subject is now the singular "the herd's drinking water"; the opening sentence now models "livestock was" so the singular and past options have a printed precedent to copy

frame: "Each [sg] and [sg]" + a phrase ending on a plural noun; tense from a before-clause
decider_quote: before the growers recognized the fungus
deletion_test: Delete "before the growers recognized the fungus and sterilized the benches": "Each graft ... was developing small brown lesions" and "is developing small brown lesions" are both acceptable; the next sentence is a present general statement and does not fix the time of the outbreak.

distractor_pulls.were developing: A compound joined by "and" is the textbook plural subject, and the tense is right; a student who has drilled "X and Y take a plural verb" picks it.
distractor_pulls.are developing: The adjacent plural "trays" and the plural "lesions" right after the blank; the present progressive also matches the present tense of the following sentence ("are especially exposed").
distractor_pulls.is developing: Correct number for a student who knows the "each" rule; the present progressive is the natural tense for describing a disease in progress, and the next sentence is in the present.

distractor_kills.were developing: Agreement: "each" before a compound subject makes it singular ("Each graft and cutting was"); correct only without "Each": "The graft and the cutting were developing."
distractor_kills.are developing: Fails agreement as above and tense: "before the growers recognized" is past; correct only in "The grafts are developing lesions before the growers notice."
distractor_kills.is developing: Tense: the past-tense time clause "before the growers recognized the fungus" requires the past; correct only with "before the growers recognize the fungus."

hostile_reader.options_only_pick: none: complete 2x2, all progressive, same length class
heuristics_that_give_key: (a) opposite of the noun before the blank
hostile_reader.changed: put the blank in the first sentence so it does not share A1/A3's second-sentence position

frame: A singular head with a numeral compound modifier + of + plural, opened by "The" (no number-marking article); aspect from a definite-past time phrase
decider_quote: on the third day of that year's monsoon
deletion_test: Delete "on the third day of that year's monsoon": "The twelve-week comparison ... has been halted by an independent board" is normal news-style present perfect, and "was halted" is fine too; the surrounding sentences are present ("kills," "remains," "blames") or a non-deciding past ("pinned").

distractor_pulls.has been halted: The present perfect is the default for reporting a halt whose report is still current, and the passage's frame is present ("kills," "remains public," "blames"); the number is right.
distractor_pulls.were halted: "the two leading candidates" sits right before the blank and is a natural thing to halt (vaccines are halted), so a reader can take the candidates as what was stopped; the tense is right.
distractor_pulls.have been halted: Joins the two pulls: the candidates as what was stopped and the present-tense report frame that favors the perfect.

distractor_kills.has been halted: Tense: the present perfect does not combine with a definite past time phrase ("on the third day of that year's monsoon"); correct only without that phrase.
distractor_kills.were halted: Agreement: the grammatical head is "comparison"; correct only as "The two leading candidates were halted."
distractor_kills.have been halted: Fails agreement with "comparison" and the definite past phrase; correct only in "The two candidates have been halted."

hostile_reader.options_only_pick: "was halted" is the shortest option, by one character over "were halted"
heuristics_that_give_key: (a) opposite of the noun before the blank
hostile_reader.changed: revision: "A" -> "The" so the article no longer marks the number; the plural attractor is now something that can itself be halted ("candidates"); the agent is longer so the time phrase sits 9 words on; the decider is a single day pinned by "that year's" instead of "during the first rainy season"; the whole passage frame is present, strengthening the perfect

frame: Ellipsis in a sentence-final though-clause; clause 1 singular subject + present perfect; the plural though-subject has a subject relative ending on singular "it"; a preceding sentence in the simple present
deletion_test: Replace "has withstood" with "withstands": "do not" becomes the correct ellipsis and "have not" fails; nothing else in the sentence fixes the auxiliary.

distractor_pulls.does not: "replaced it" ends right at the blank, so a reader who takes the nearest pronoun as the subject hears "it does not"; do-support is also the everyday ellipsis, and the first sentence's verbs ("spreads," "blackens") are simple present.
distractor_pulls.do not: "though they do not" is the default spoken ellipsis and agrees with "cultivars"; the first sentence supplies simple-present verbs a reader can think it stands for.
distractor_pulls.has not: The singular "it" sits immediately before the blank, and "has" is the auxiliary printed in the main clause; it reads as "it has not."

distractor_kills.does not: Ellipsis and agreement: the elided verb is the perfect "withstood," which needs "have," and the though-clause's subject is the plural "cultivars"; correct only after "a russet withstands scab, though the cultivar that replaced it does not."
distractor_kills.do not: Ellipsis: do-support stands for a simple-present lexical verb, but the antecedent in the same sentence is "has withstood"; correct only after "a single russet withstands three such summers."
distractor_kills.has not: Agreement: "it" is the object of "replaced"; the subject is "cultivars"; correct only with "though the cultivar that replaced it has not."

heuristics_that_give_key: none of (a)-(f): the noun before is plural and the key plural; the first noun is singular
hostile_reader.changed: revision: the blank now follows a subject relative ending on singular "it" ("the cultivars that replaced it"), so the number is no longer read off a plural noun at the blank; added an opening present-simple sentence so do-support has a printed candidate; moved the blank out of the first sentence

frame: Possessive split: opening because-clause subject is the singular owner; plural head + from-phrase ending on a singular noun + verb + its/their; the possessed thing is something people could carry
decider_quote: the district's lone health clinic floods
deletion_test: Delete the because-clause: "nurses from the mainland hospital's outreach program have moved their vaccine refrigerator" becomes fully acceptable (the nurses' own refrigerator); only the flooding clinic makes the refrigerator the clinic's.

distractor_pulls.has moved their: "program" right before the blank pulls the verb to "has," and nurses running an outreach program plausibly carry their own vaccine supply.
distractor_pulls.has moved its: Everything right before the blank is singular ("the mainland hospital's outreach program"); "its" then reads as the program's refrigerator, a smooth singular sentence.
distractor_pulls.have moved their: The verb is right, and it is natural for the people doing the moving to be moving their own equipment; outreach nurses do carry vaccines, so a reader need not look back at the clinic.

distractor_kills.has moved their: Agreement: the head is "nurses"; and the refrigerator is the flooding clinic's. Correct only with a plural owner earlier: "Because the district's clinics flood, the program has moved their refrigerator."
distractor_kills.has moved its: Agreement: the head of the subject is the plural "nurses," not "program"; correct only as "the outreach program has moved its refrigerator."
distractor_kills.have moved their: Pronoun-antecedent: the because-clause gives the reason the refrigerator is moved, so it belongs to the singular "clinic"; correct only after "Because the district's health clinics flood."

heuristics_that_give_key: (a) opposite of the noun before the blank
(f) does NOT apply as a counter: every pronoun row in this batch is split by design, a batch-level tell I cannot remove from inside the row
hostile_reader.changed: revision: new topic and owned noun; the possessed thing is equipment people could carry ("vaccine refrigerator"), so "their" is a believable reading until the because-clause is used; no part-of-a-pond noun after the blank; the owner is now the because-clause SUBJECT but carries no "only"-type cue beside the possessed word

frame: Object pronoun: clause 1 (before a semicolon) names the singular referent and a plural rival; clause 2's plural subject + phrase ending on a singular noun + blank; the referent is fixed by a fact 10+ words after the blank
decider_quote: The cholera vaccine is the only heat-stable product
deletion_test: Delete "The cholera vaccine is the only heat-stable product among" (leaving "The three oral vaccines are on the ministry's list"): "carry them" becomes the only reading; nothing else singles out one vaccine.

distractor_pulls.carries it: "the hill district" right before the blank is singular, and the whole first clause is about one vaccine; read fast, the sentence is singular throughout.
distractor_pulls.carry them: The nearest vaccine noun to the blank is the plural "the three oral vaccines on the ministry's list," which health workers plausibly carry; the plural verb and plural pronoun read as a matched pair.
distractor_pulls.carries them: A reader who takes "district" as subject and picks up the nearer plural "three oral vaccines" as the thing carried.

distractor_kills.carries it: Agreement: the subject is "health workers"; correct only with "the district's health worker carries it."
distractor_kills.carry them: Pronoun-antecedent: only the heat-stable vaccine can travel in shoulder bags to villages with no electricity; the last sentence says the other two need cold boxes. Correct only if all three vaccines were heat-stable.
distractor_kills.carries them: Fails both; correct only in "a health worker carries them" with three heat-stable vaccines.

hostile_reader.options_only_pick: "carry it" is the shortest option (8 vs 10/10/12 characters), a weak tell
heuristics_that_give_key: (a) opposite of the noun before the blank
hostile_reader.changed: revision: no echo pronoun for the referent in clause 1 ("its sap" removed) and no later restatement of it in the blank's sentence ("the plant" removed); the referent is now the first-clause SUBJECT with a plural rival ("the three oral vaccines") nearer the blank; what decides the pronoun is a fact 10+ words after the blank ("no electricity") plus the next sentence, not a word next to it

frame: Singular head + comma-set appositive ending on a plural noun, blank, commaless adverbial ("in the clinic's experience") + "rarely if ever", then an intransitive participle
misleader_words: usually a handful of scaly patches on the wrists
deletion_test: Replace "recurred" with "serious": "is in the clinic's experience rarely if ever serious" becomes correct and "has" fails; nothing else decides be vs have.

distractor_pulls.is: "Contact dermatitis ... is in the clinic's experience rarely if ever" is the commonest frame for describing a condition ("is rarely serious"); the copula reading survives for seven words, through "rarely if ever," until "recurred."
distractor_pulls.have: "a handful of" is a quantity expression that takes a plural verb ("a handful of patches have appeared"), so the appositive seems to fix a plural; and "have" is the right auxiliary for the participle.
distractor_pulls.are: The plural "wrists" and "patches" sit right before the blank, and "are in the clinic's experience rarely if ever" reads as describing the patches.

distractor_kills.is: Verb form: "recur" is intransitive, so "is recurred" is ungrammatical; correct only with an adjective: "is ... rarely if ever serious."
distractor_kills.have: Agreement: an appositive does not change the subject's number; the head is "dermatitis." Correct only as "The scaly patches have rarely if ever recurred."
distractor_kills.are: Fails agreement and verb form; correct only in "The patches are rarely if ever serious."

heuristics_that_give_key: (a) opposite of the noun before the blank
hostile_reader.changed: revision: the participle moved from 5 to 8 words after the blank, behind "in the clinic's experience rarely if ever", where "is"/"are" still read as the start of a description ("is rarely serious"); new head ("dermatitis") and new appositive; generic subject instead of one worker

frame: Sentence-final restrictive participial phrase; another sentence establishes several sets of the noun; no subset cue ("only") in the blank's sentence
structure: "the samples" + restrictive participial phrase "drawn in the barn nearest the duck pond"; only the first sentence (four barns) makes the phrase identifying rather than additional
decider_quote: in all four barns of one poultry farm

distractor_pulls.samples, drawn: With no "only" in the sentence, "retested the samples, drawn in the barn nearest the duck pond" reads as retesting all the samples and then adding where they came from, a common shape for a sentence-final participle.
distractor_pulls.samples—drawn: A single dash before a final explanatory phrase is correct in form, and inside this sentence nothing contradicts one set of samples.
distractor_pulls.samples drawn,: Reads as a pause before the location phrase.

distractor_kills.samples, drawn: Makes the phrase nonrestrictive, so all the samples were drawn in that barn; the first sentence says blood came from all four barns. Correct only if one barn had been sampled.
distractor_kills.samples—drawn: Same nonrestrictive reading as the comma; correct only if the inspectors had sampled a single barn.
distractor_kills.samples drawn,: Separates the participle "drawn" from its locative complement "in the barn"; no convention allows that comma.

hostile_reader.options_only_pick: "samples drawn," can be struck at a glance (the row allows one)
hostile_reader.changed: revision: removed "only" and "To settle the question cheaply", which both announced a subset inside the blank's sentence; the subset reading now rests entirely on sentence 1, and the middle sentence gives a reason to retest without implying a part
